claims.text: At high temperature, differences in surface diffusion rates among constituent elements drive early elemental segregation at nanoparticle surfaces and grain boundaries.
Surface and grain-boundary segregation leads to phase separation that compromises structural and chemical stability.
High-temperature instability is especially pronounced in nanoparticles with low noble-metal content.
The initial nanoparticles are homogeneous, single-phase, near-equiatomic multielement solid solutions.
The nanoparticles can be tested by in situ TEM-EDS during controlled temperature ramps of 773–1173 K and 473–1923 K.
Using an inert atmosphere and low noble-metal content isolates diffusion-driven instability.
Compositional inhomogeneities will first emerge at surfaces and grain boundaries and will be followed by secondary-phase formation.
At elevated temperature, elements with higher surface diffusivity migrate faster than the other constituent elements.
Differential diffusion creates local elemental enrichments and depletions that nucleate segregation and phase separation.
Annealing or temperature changes can decompose near-equiatomic high-entropy solid solutions into multiple phases.
High-temperature samples will show more compositional gradients and distinct phase boundaries than room-temperature or low-temperature controls.
Nanoparticles maintained below the threshold for significant atomic mobility will retain uniform elemental dispersion.
The proposed mechanism applies to near-equiatomic multielement nanoparticles with minimal noble-metal content.
Higher noble-metal fractions or different particle sizes may permit alternative stabilization mechanisms to dominate.
Adding noble metal provides a controlled test of the effect of composition on diffusion rates and segregation.
Absence of a segregation or phase-separation difference between high- and low-temperature samples would falsify the predicted temperature-dependent instability.
Absence of a difference between low-noble-metal and noble-metal-enriched samples would falsify differential surface diffusion as the cause of instability.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis states that it is unclear how noble-metal content changes the onset or extent of phase separation, yet the falsification rule requires a difference between low- and higher-noble-metal samples and treats no difference as falsifying the entire diffusion mechanism.
